Pestilence
pes'ti-lens
n. (a deadly epidemic; rendering Hebrew deber, Greek loimos)
From the Latin pestilentia, from pestis, a plague. Hebrew deber is a plague or murrain, and it stands in the prophets as one of a standing set of covenant judgments — sword, famine, pestilence, and the noisome beast — announced together as God's four sore judgments.

Biblical Definition

Pestilence is deadly epidemic disease, and Scripture treats it as one of God's instruments rather than as an event outside his government. Ezekiel names the standing set: “my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast” (Ezekiel 14:21). It falls after David's sin in numbering the people, and the narrative is careful to attribute it directly: “So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning even to the time appointed” (2 Samuel 24:15) — and equally careful to record that it stopped at a threshingfloor where an altar was built and sacrifice offered. Jeremiah announces it as the answer to a people whose religion had become formality: “when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence” (Jeremiah 14:12). Yet the Psalter promises the believer God's protection in exactly the same vocabulary: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psalm 91:3). Both are true, and both are God's doing.

Webster 1828 Definition

A deadly epidemic. Scripture lists it among God's four sore judgments with sword, famine, and beast — and in the same vocabulary promises deliverance from the noisome pestilence.

expand to see more

PESTILENCE, n. [L. pestilentia, from pestis, plague.] Plague; an infectious or contagious disease of a malignant and destructive kind.

2. Corruption; moral disease destructive to happiness; as, the pestilence of error.

3. Anything that is noxious to morals or to the peace of society.

4. In Scripture, one of the four sore judgments; as, the sword, the famine, the noisome beast, and the pestilence, Ezek. 14.

5. Of deliverance; as, he shall deliver thee from the noisome pestilence, Psa. 91.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 14:21 — "For thus saith the Lord GOD; How much more when I send my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast?"

2 Samuel 24:15 — "So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning even to the time appointed: and there died of the people from Dan even to Beersheba seventy thousand men."

Psalm 91:3 — "Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence."

Jeremiah 14:12 — "When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence."

Modern Corruption

Epidemic disease is either explained wholly by second causes with no Governor above them, or else read as a targeted verdict on the individuals it reaches. Scripture affirms God's hand and forbids the confident private verdict.

expand to see more

The naturalist frame is not wrong about mechanisms — contagion has causes, and Scripture itself legislated quarantine in Leviticus 13 long before germ theory. The error is treating a full account of second causes as a complete account. Amos asks whether there is evil in a city and the LORD hath not done it, and 2 Samuel 24:15 says plainly that the LORD sent the pestilence. Providence is not confined to what medicine cannot explain.

The opposite error reads a plague as a scoreboard and assigns guilt to the dead. Our Lord forbids exactly this reasoning about those on whom the tower in Siloam fell: think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. The principle to recover is that a judgment in the earth is a summons to everyone who hears of it rather than a verdict on those it struck. And Psalm 91:3 keeps the believer's confidence where it belongs: not in immunity, but in a God who delivers, and who did not spare his own Son.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew deber is pestilence or murrain, and maggephah is a plague or stroke. Greek loimos is a pestilence, listed by our Lord among the signs preceding the end.

expand to see more

Hebrew deber (H1698) — pestilence, plague; one of the four sore judgments.

Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a stroke, a plague; the plague that stopped at the threshingfloor.

Hebrew negeph (H5063) — a blow, a plague; that there be no plague among them, Exodus 30:12.

Greek loimos (G3061) — a pestilence; there shall be famines, and pestilences, Matthew 24:7.

Greek plege (G4127) — a stroke, a plague, a wound; the plagues of Revelation.

Usage

"Of the four sore judgments: the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence (Ezekiel 14:21)."

"Of God's direct hand after David's sin: so the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel (2 Samuel 24:15)."

"Of deliverance promised: he shall deliver thee… from the noisome pestilence (Psalm 91:3)."
